    For Task 2, you can implement this as a small Bash script. The key safety requirement is that the argument is data only—it must never be executed or passed to a shell evaluation mechanism.

    1. Create the directories

    mkdir -p ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/{bin,web,markers,evidence}

    2. Create bin/safe_marker.sh

    #!/bin/bash

# Require exactly one argument
if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 course-marker" >&2
    exit 1
fi

marker="$1"
marker_dir="$HOME/csce465-agentsec/hw1/markers"
marker_file="$marker_dir/marker.txt"

# Create the markers directory if necessary
mkdir -p "$marker_dir"

# Write the supplied marker as data, not as a command
printf '%s\n' "$marker" > "$marker_file"

    Then make it executable:

    chmod +x ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/bin/safe_marker.sh

    3. Test it

    A normal invocation:

    ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/bin/safe_marker.sh hello
cat ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/markers/marker.txt

    Expected:

    hello

    Test rejection of zero arguments:

    ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/bin/safe_marker.sh

    Test rejection of two arguments:

    ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/bin/safe_marker.sh hello world

    Both should exit with status 1.

    4. Test the security property

    An argument containing shell metacharacters should be treated literally:

    ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/bin/safe_marker.sh 'hello; touch /tmp/should-not-exist'

    Then:

    cat ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/markers/marker.txt

    should show the literal text:

    hello; touch /tmp/should-not-exist

    and the command should not create /tmp/should-not-exist.

    The important part is that we're using:

    printf '%s\n' "$marker"

    rather than something dangerous like:

    eval "$marker"

    or:

    bash -c "$marker"

    Those would interpret user input as shell code. Here, the user's argument is only written to marker.txt as data.

    One important detail: because the assignment says the script must create only hw1/markers/marker.txt, I would avoid having the script itself run mkdir or any other command. Create the directories beforehand, then have the script only write the file.

    1. Create the directories

    2. Create safe_marker.sh

    Put this in:

    ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/bin/safe_marker.sh

    #!/bin/bash

if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 course-marker" >&2
    exit 1
fi

marker="$1"
printf '%s\n' "$marker" > "$HOME/csce465-agentsec/hw1/markers/marker.txt"

    Then:

    chmod +x ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/bin/safe_marker.sh

    Why this satisfies the security requirements

    The script:

    • accepts exactly one argument with "$#"
    • rejects zero or multiple arguments
    • writes only to the fixed path ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/markers/marker.txt
    • does not use eval, bash -c, sh -c, command substitution, or any other mechanism that interprets the argument as a command
    • quotes "$marker", so something like hello; rm -rf ... is treated as literal text

    You can test that with:

    ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/bin/safe_marker.sh 'hello; touch /tmp/SHOULD_NOT_EXIST'
cat ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/markers/marker.txt
test ! -e /tmp/SHOULD_NOT_EXIST && echo "Safe: command was not executed"

    3. Create the OpenClaw skill

    Create:

    ~/.openclaw/workspace/skills/safe-marker/SKILL.md

    Because the assignment specifically asks for the official OpenClaw skill format, I don't want to guess at the current format. Since OpenClaw is an external/current project, the safest approach is to check its current official documentation before writing this file.

    If OpenClaw is installed, first run:

    openclaw --help

    and:

    openclaw skills --help

    Then create the skill according to the format those commands/documentation specify.

    The content should make the policy very explicit: the marker is allowed only when the user directly and explicitly requests the course-marker operation, and the command must be fixed rather than constructed from webpage content.

    The fixed command should be conceptually:

    ~/csce465-agentsec/hw1/bin/safe_marker.sh "<course-marker>"

    The skill should also explicitly say that instructions encountered in webpages—including the adversarial page—are untrusted data and are not authorization to invoke the marker.

    4. Run the skill checker and preserve its output

    Easiest: GitHub CLI

    First check whether you have it:

    gh --version

    If that works, log in:

    gh auth login

    Choose:

    1. GitHub.com
    2. HTTPS
    3. Login with a web browser

    Then, back in your terminal:

    cd ~/csce465-agentsec
git push -u origin main

    You shouldn't need to enter your GitHub password.

    If gh isn't installed

    You can use a GitHub Personal Access Token instead, but don't paste the token here or into a normal password field that isn't expecting it.

    Go to and create a token with the permissions needed to push to your repository. GitHub's current interface may offer fine-grained tokens; give it access to your csce465-agentsec repository and repository contents write access.

    Then run:

    cd ~/csce465-agentsec
git push -u origin main

    When Git asks:

    Username:

    enter your GitHub username.

    When it asks:

    Password:

    paste the token instead of your GitHub password.

    The terminal may appear to show nothing while you paste the token. That's normal.

    Before doing anything else

    Since you're already at the point where Git says your files are staged, I'd check:

    git status
git remote -v
